items.headline: CORTIS Returns to No. 1 on Billboard World Albums Chart as NMIXX and JxJ Debut
items.dek: GREENGREEN leads the chart for a sixth week, while new releases from NMIXX, SEVENTEEN’s JxJ, K/DA and ILLIT enter the top 10.
body: CORTIS is back at No. 1 on Billboard’s World Albums chart for the week ending November 7. The group’s EP “GREENGREEN” returned to the top for its sixth week in the position and re-entered the Billboard 200 six months after its release.
CORTIS also charted with debut EP “COLOR OUTSIDE THE LINES,” which placed No. 22 in its 60th week on the World Albums chart.
Stray Kids held three spots, led by “THIS & THAT” at No. 2 in its 12th week. “KARMA” ranked No. 9 in its 59th week, while “DO IT” came in at No. 18 in its 41st.
Two new releases followed at Nos. 3 and 4: NMIXX’s EP “Strange Muse” and “DREAMSCAPE,” the debut mini album from SEVENTEEN unit JxJ, made up of Jeonghan and Joshua.

ENHYPEN’s “THE SIN : BLISS” placed No. 5 in its 10th week. League of Legends virtual group K/DA debuted at No. 6 with “FIRESTARTER,” while ILLIT’s “BREAK EVEN” entered at No. 7 ahead of its U.S. physical release. ILLIT’s earlier mini album “MAMIHLAPINATAPAI” ranked No. 13 in its 26th week.
BTS also had two albums on the chart: “Map of the Soul: 7 ~The Journey~” at No. 12 and “Love Yourself: Answer,” which re-entered at No. 15 for its 206th week.

Further down, ATEEZ’s “GOLDEN HOUR : Part.5” ranked No. 16, followed by NewJeans’ “Get Up” at No. 17 and BOYNEXTDOOR’s “HOME” at No. 19. LE SSERAFIM’s “PUREFLOW” placed No. 21, and EVAN (Heeseung)’s “DEATH OF ME” came in at No. 24.

items.headline: The Philippine K-pop Concert Guide: Every 2026-2027 Show, Venue and Ticket Link
items.dek: Multiple K-pop shows are headed to the Philippines from November 2026 to March 2027, from HUTA's Heat Max to three sold-out BTS nights in Bulacan. Here is every date, venue and official ticket link in one place.
body: Sixteen K-pop shows are on the calendar for the Philippines between November 2026 and March 2027, and the HallyuScope concert calendar tracks every one of them, with the poster, seat plan and official ticket link for each show. Here is the full rundown, month by month.

November opens with LEE MINHYUK (HUTA), who brings his HEAT MAX tour to the SM North EDSA Skydome in Quezon City on November 21, then PENTAGON's 10th anniversary tour, 101010, at the Aliw Theater in Pasay on November 29. Both shows are on sale through Ticketmaster Philippines. One date fans should cross off: OMEGA X's November 28 Manila show was cancelled in September, and the promoter is processing refunds.

December has a genuine clash. PARK JINYOUNG plays his first concert tour, CODE#, at the FYM Hall in the EVM Convention Center, Quezon City, on December 5, with tickets through Tap Your Tickets, and LE SSERAFIM brings its PUREFLOW tour to the SM Mall of Asia Arena the same night, both at 7:00 PM, so it is a one-or-the-other decision. LE SSERAFIM's December 6 show was cancelled and its ticket holders were moved to December 5. NCT 127 follows with NEO CITY, THE REDLINE at the MOA Arena on December 12 at 5:00 PM, and ROCKY closes the year with his Fake It fan concert at Samsung Hall, SM Aura in Taguig on December 20, on sale through Ticketmaster Philippines.

January brings three different flavours. JACOB of THE BOYZ plays his More Than Words fan concert at the Music Museum in San Juan on January 19 at 8:00 PM. DOH KYUNG SOO brings his DAY OFF concert tour to the Smart Araneta Coliseum on January 23, with tickets through TicketNet. KATSEYE's THE WILDWORLD TOUR reaches the MOA Arena on January 29. The Manila date is already sold out on Ticketmaster, so the Cebu stop is the one to watch.

February is the month of the double booking. KATSEYE plays the SM Seaside Cebu Arena on February 7, and on February 20 BIGBANG returns to the Philippines for the first time since 2015 with XX: COSMOS at the SMDC Festival Grounds in Parañaque, while Young K of DAY6 brings his solo tour, YOUNGEST, to the New Frontier Theater in Quezon City the same night.

March belongs to BTS. The group's ARIRANG world tour plays three nights at the Philippine Sports Stadium in Bulacan, March 13, 14 and 16, and all three are sold out. The March 16 date was added after the first two sold out in June 2026. A week later, EXO-KASE, the new unit of EXO's Kai and Sehun, brings its SILENT CITY fan concert tour to the Smart Araneta Coliseum on March 21. Ticket details have not been announced yet.

Two things worth knowing before you buy. First, every ticket link on the HallyuScope concert calendar goes to the official seller for that show, Ticketmaster Philippines, SM Tickets, TicketNet, Tap Your Tickets or Megatix, so a link that is not on the calendar is not one we have verified. Second, prices and statuses change: the calendar shows each show's prices as announced, and it is updated as shows sell out, move or are added.

items.headline: Ticketing day, minus the panic
items.dek: The checklist to finish before a Philippine K-pop ticket sale opens, so the queue is the only thing left to worry about.
body: A ticket sale is won before it opens. The fans who get in are usually the ones who did the boring prep the night before, and this guide is that prep, in order.

Start with the official seller. The promoter's announcement always names it, and every show on the HallyuScope concert calendar links straight to that page. In the Philippines it is usually Ticketmaster PH, SM Tickets or TicketNet, with Tap Your Tickets and Megatix handling some shows. If a link does not lead to the named seller or the promoter's own page, do not trust it. Resellers and random social media sellers are where fans lose money.

Check for presales. Many tours open a fan club or membership presale a few days before the general sale, and some promoters or card partners run their own. Presales usually need a code or a verified membership, and that verification can close days before the sale itself, so read the promoter's announcement as soon as the tour is posted.

Make the account the night before. Create an account on the seller's site, save your details, and log in once so you know the password works. Big sales put everyone in an online queue or waiting room. Stay on one tab and do not refresh, because refreshing usually sends you to the back of the line.

Sort out payment early. Check which cards and e-wallets the seller accepts, make sure your card works for online payments, and know your daily limit. Many failed checkouts are a declined payment, not a sold-out section, and a timed-out cart usually goes back into the pool.

Know the sale time in Manila time, and the ticket limit per account. Sales open at a set hour and the big ones sell out fast. Be in the queue a few minutes early with your device charged and on a stable connection.

Have a backup plan, not a backup seller. Decide your section and your price ceiling before the queue opens, so you are not deciding while the clock runs. If your first choice sells out, take the next best seat in the same sale rather than chasing a second site. Keep the confirmation email and the ticket QR somewhere you can reach without signal, because venue gates are not kind to dead batteries.
items.socialCaption: Ticketing day does not have to be a panic. The checklist is short, do it the night before, and the queue is the only thing left. Read the guide on HallyuScope.

items.headline: Your first K-pop concert in Manila
items.dek: Venues, entry times, lightsticks, and the etiquette nobody tells you before your first show.
body: Your first K-pop concert in Manila is equal parts show and logistics, and the logistics are the part nobody warns you about. This is the short version of what to know before the day.

The shows rotate through the same venues. SM Mall of Asia Arena in Pasay hosts most big arena tours, and the Philippine Sports Stadium in Bulacan takes the stadium-sized ones. Smart Araneta Coliseum in Quezon City hosts mid-size shows, while New Frontier Theater, Aliw Theater, SM North EDSA Skydome, FYM Hall at EVM Convention Center and Music Museum cover the rest. Check the venue on the calendar before you plan the trip, because the same artist can play a different venue each tour.

Read the house rules before you pack. The promoter posts them a few days before the show: bag size, what you can bring in, and whether cameras are allowed. Professional cameras and big power banks are often not allowed, and food and drinks usually are not. If a bag check is listed, pack light.

Evening shows start between 5 and 8 PM, and doors usually open an hour or two before that. Leave early. Manila traffic does not care about your lightstick, and the queues for entry, merch and the official lightstick booth are all longer than you expect. Bring a valid ID and your ticket, digital or printed, and keep both where you can reach them.

The lightstick is the uniform. If the group has one, bring it, charged, with spare batteries, and pair it with the official app before you arrive if it syncs to the show. The crowd does the rest: fan chants during the songs, banners during the ballads, and a sea of light during the encore. If you do not know the chants, listen for a song or two first. Nobody minds a quiet first-timer, and everyone minds a camera flash in a dark arena.
Look out for fan freebies. Fan clubs often hand out banners, photocards or slogans near the venue before doors open. They are free and run by fans, so be patient in line, and say thank you.

After the show, the venue empties slowly. Plan your ride home before the encore, not after it. Ride hailing surges around the arena, so a pre-booked car or a meetup point a short walk away saves the wait. And keep your ticket stub. Your first concert becomes the one you measure every other concert against.

items.headline: Album versions, POBs and inclusions
items.dek: A plain-language breakdown of versions, pre-order benefits, and what actually comes inside a K-pop album.
body: A K-pop album is not one product. It is a set of versions, each with different covers, different photocards and sometimes different extras, and the pre-order benefit is a whole second layer on top. Here is what each part means.

Versions are the choices. Most releases come in two or more versions, usually a different cover and a different photocard set per version. Some are member versions, where each version is dedicated to one member. Buying every version is a collector's choice, not a requirement. One version gets you the album, the songs and a full set of inclusions.

Formats change what is in the box. A photobook version is the big one, with the most inclusions. Jewel case and digipack versions are smaller and cheaper, with fewer extras. Platform albums, such as Weverse Albums or Nemo albums, come with no CD at all: you get a card or a small package with a code that unlocks the music and digital photos in an app.

Inclusions are what comes inside the album. The standard set is a photobook, a CD and a random photocard, plus extras that change by release: a poster, stickers, a lyrics booklet or a postcard. The random photocard is the part fans trade. It is one member out of the group, pulled at random, and trading is half the hobby.

POB stands for pre-order benefit. It is an extra photocard, or a small set of extras, given only to fans who order before the release date, and only from the shop that offers it. Each shop has its own POB, so the same album pre-ordered from two shops comes with two different extra photocards. That is why fans compare shops before they buy.

Where you buy matters. Official shops and the group's own store are the safe baseline. Local Philippine sellers, both online shops and physical stores, often carry the same versions and run group orders that split international shipping. Check the version name, the shop's POB and the release date before you pay, ask whether the POB is guaranteed or while supplies last, and keep the order confirmation until the album is in your hands.

items.headline: What to bring (and what to skip) at a K-pop concert in Manila
items.dek: The packing list, the banned items, the dos and don'ts, and the outfit, all in one place.
body: This is the checklist version of our first concert guide. Read it before you leave the house, because once you are in the queue, the things you forgot are the things you will miss most.

What to bring: your ticket, digital or printed, and a valid ID. A phone, charged, and a small power bank, because the promoter sets a size limit and a big one may not get through the door. Your lightstick, charged, with spare batteries. A small bag that fits the venue size limit, with cash and a card inside. Earplugs if loud sound bothers you. Keep the essentials in one small pouch so the bag check is fast.

What to leave at home: professional cameras and lenses, big power banks, selfie sticks, laser pointers, large bags and backpacks, outside food and drinks, and umbrellas, since most indoor venues do not allow them past the door. Skip anything that blocks the view of the person behind you. The promoter posts the house rules a few days before the show, and the rules are the final word. If it is on the banned list, security will hold it or turn you away.

The dos: arrive early, learn the fan chants, and keep your lightstick at chest height during the show so the people behind you can see. Stay hydrated, keep your ticket and ID where you can reach them, and follow the ushers. If you are in a standing section, know your number and your spot, and keep your things close. Trade photocards and banners politely, in the areas where trading is allowed.

The don'ts: no flash photography, no holding your phone above your head for the whole song, no pushing toward the stage, and no recording when the promoter says no recording. Do not buy tickets from scalpers outside the venue, and do not leave rubbish in your seat. The fastest way to ruin a stranger's night is a bright screen in a dark arena.

What to wear: comfortable shoes first, because you will queue, stand, and walk a lot. Light layers work best. It is hot and humid outside and cold inside the arena once the air conditioning is on. Wear merch or the group colors if you like, but skip oversized hats, tall headbands, and anything with lights that stay on during the show. A small crossbody bag beats a backpack at the bag check and in a crowded row.

The Manila part: rain. If it is raining, bring a poncho for the queue outside, because the line forms outdoors at most venues. Leave hours early for traffic, and plan your ride home before the encore, because ride hailing surges around the arena when thousands of people leave at once. A meetup point a short walk away beats waiting at the gate.

Check the concert calendar for the venue and the show time, read the promoter house rules the day before, and pack the night before. The show is the easy part. Getting there ready is the work, and it is worth it.
